Part Four: Substance, its basic kinds, and their properties

It is surprising that the author of The Eastern Discussions, after repeating these ideas in his books and commentaries on the philosophers, later says that they could defend their view this way: anything that exists in something else can be considered as being in a subject or as being in a compound. The second way does not make it an accident, since it is a part, and an accident cannot be a part. The first way—being in a subject—must mean either that the subject is constituted by what exists in it or that it is not.
Part Four: Substance, its basic kinds, and their properties

The first possibility is false for two reasons. First, what exists in the subject depends on the subject. If the subject also depended on it, each would depend on the other, creating a circle. Second, the matter of the elements is shared by their different forms. If the existence of any one elemental form helped constitute the matter, then when that form disappeared, the matter would disappear too. The matter would no longer be shared, which is impossible. This would make what exists in the subject both substance and accident. That is the difficulty raised by those who allow one thing to be both.
Part Four: Substance, its basic kinds, and their properties

The answer is to recall what we have already said. First, this argument confuses substance with substantiality—that is, being essential—and accident with being incidental, or outside the essence. It argues that anything in a subject is a substance because it is a part of the whole. But a part of the whole is not incidental to that whole; that does not mean it is not an accident in itself. Being a part does not make something a substance in itself, only essential to something else. So a thing can be an accident in itself and substantial to something else without contradiction.
Part Four: Substance, its basic kinds, and their properties

Second, the argument again confuses a thing’s state in itself with its relation to something else. It reasons from the denial of one relation to the affirmation of its opposite. But it is wrong to infer that something is a substance because it is not incidental. The opposite of “incidental” is “essential,” not “substance.” A thing can be essential to something without being a substance in itself. Color, for example, is essential to blackness but is not a substance.
Part Four: Substance, its basic kinds, and their properties

Third, the circle it describes is not always impossible. The form that constitutes matter and the matter constituted by it depend on one another in different respects, as we will explain in the discussion of how matter and form are connected. Not every relation called a circle—even if the same word is used—has the same kind of dependence on both sides. Only a circle in which both sides depend on each other in the same respect is impossible. That is what the proof rules out, not every relation that can be called circular.
Part Four: Substance, its basic kinds, and their properties

Fourth, as we will explain, matter depends for its existence as a subject on some form or other, but it does not depend on any accident in this way. This is the basis for distinguishing form from accident. An accident is a descriptive feature that cannot exist unless its subject supports it. A substantial form needs a subject only because of the conditions that make it an individual and the requirements of its existence in the outside world.
Part Four: Substance, its basic kinds, and their properties
Let this be the end of what we set out to say about substance and accident. Here ends the first volume of the Second Journey; the second volume follows, God willing.

Delaying the discussion of substances until after accidents does not mean that knowledge of substances belongs in divine science. It may mean only that this knowledge belongs close to, and in connection with, divine science.

“Knowledge of substances” means knowing substances as what accidents depend on. This belongs more naturally in the study of divine realities than in a first philosophy that studies general concepts. The relation of accidents to substances is like the relation of concepts to essences; knowledge of accidents therefore comes before knowledge of substances, just as general philosophy comes before divine science.
The commentator says this was Ibn Sahlān al-Sāwijī, though the teacher he asked could not confirm the name.

An objection: even if the argument works, it would require the thing related to also be one of the seven relational categories. But that is not so. Place, for example, is not itself a category in the way the argument needs, nor is time. The same applies to the other cases. One might reply that a category follows, in some sense, the broader kind of what it relates to; still, there seems to be no single essential feature shared by all these relations.

This does not show that unity and a point are outside quantity in every sense. At most, a point is outside continuous quantity and unity outside discrete quantity. That is enough to undermine the claim that either is a starting point for all quantity. No one says that a point, as discrete quantity, is the beginning of the continuous, or that unity, as continuous quantity, is the beginning of the discrete. This also shows why the Sheikh's answer to the objection is not sound.

In short, heaviness and lightness are divisible only incidentally, while quantity itself is divisible by nature. The argument fails because it shifts its key claim: if it says heaviness is divisible only incidentally, it has not shown that heaviness is quantity by nature. If it says heaviness is divisible by nature, that claim is false.

“Arrangement” here means that the parts are distinct in existence but coexist. Time has no position because its parts do not exist together. Number has no position because its parts are not continuous.
The odd is simply what is not even. That is why this description can also apply to the Necessary Being. The two oppose each other as affirmation and negation.
The parts of an element can be continuous with other parts of the same kind. A celestial sphere, by contrast, can be continuous with another body only through their shared broader kind.

Even a little reflection shows the problem with the replies to the second and third ways of matching. It is astonishing that the author, for all his standing among scholars, should have said this. Think carefully, and the point will become clear. — Fath Ali Khoyi.

This refers to the proof by matching. It says that two infinite distances must differ by greater and smaller amounts if one contains the other. But if a greater and a smaller infinite distance can be compared this way, then both must be finite. The same reasoning applies to the example used against the proof.

The same argument that says an infinite body acts in no time by acting on a large part also says this if we consider a smaller part, and indeed every part, when the thing acted on is finite. The action in no time on the large part would then be faster than the action in no time on the smaller part. So the contradiction is no clearer in the second case.

The thought is that if the parts of the cause act on the parts of the thing affected in no time, then the whole cause would act on the whole thing in no time too—even though we assumed that this happens over time.

If the surface were a part of the body, it would have to be either a defining feature or a form, not a material part or a general kind. A material part or general kind is substance taken either apart from other features or without excluding them. A defining feature or form is what completes a thing and makes it actual. But a surface, considered as the body's end, does not complete the body. It is the body's limit, cut, or boundary, though it exists in the body and not in something else. So it is an accident of a finite natural body, but not of a geometrical body, whose three dimensions are already complete.

There are two objections. First, an accident cannot exist in another accident. Second, a geometrical surface is not something outside the three dimensions of geometrical body: we obtain it by considering two dimensions without the third. Once we set the third aside, what separate subject is left for the surface to exist in? This is how our teacher explained it, though the first objection needs further thought. — Fath Ali Khoyi.

A point is the end of a line that has only one dimension, so the point itself has no dimension. In the same way, a line is the end of a surface with two dimensions and therefore has one; a surface is the end of a body with three dimensions and therefore has two. — Avicenna.
The moving body seeks place through its movement. Place must therefore exist while it moves; otherwise, it would be seeking something that does not exist.

Place as a dimensioned substance has position. Immaterial substances such as intellect and soul do not. The argument proves only that place is not an immaterial substance; it does not rule out every kind of substance.
The comparison is not exact. “Known” is not formed from “knowledge” in the same way, because “knowledge” names an act, while “known” names what receives that act.

If this dimension were material, it would be a form; but, as we have seen, a form cannot be place. Also, if the dimension were material, the dimension and matter together would form a body, which would itself need a place. Its place could not be a part of the first body's dimension, since it would move with it. It would therefore have to be part of another body, which would also need a place that was not the dimension belonging to the first body; otherwise, material substances would overlap. That place would be another dimension belonging to a third body, and so on without end. This would mean an infinite regress of dimensions, which earlier arguments have ruled out. Think carefully. — Ismail.

This completes both examples and qualifies both claims. It is what makes the first example a genuine objection. In the second example, either this point or the fact that both surfaces are concave completes the objection. — Fath.

If “infinite” means “not finite” in a sense that applies only to things that could be finite, we can say that these dimensions are neither finite nor infinite. A subject that cannot have either feature can be free of both, just as the First Intellect is neither blind nor sighted. And even if infinity in this sense is ruled out, finitude has not thereby been proved. If “infinite” simply means “not finite,” we can say that the dimensions are not finite in this broad sense. Denying finitude does not prove that they are infinite in the other sense, so the earlier proofs would not refute them.

Now suppose they are finite and have shape. The claim that the shape belongs to them by their own nature does not mean that the part must have the same shape as the whole. That would follow only if they had parts and wholes, but parts and wholes result from division, which requires matter—whether the division is real or imagined. A thing without matter cannot be divided. We may instead say that an agent gives them shape without matter. The claim that this would make them ready for division, joining, and stretching is not established; it would follow only if shape could arise in those three ways and no others. A thing might receive its shape from its original nature, without any division, joining, or stretching. If it naturally excludes other shapes, there is no arbitrary choice of one shape over another. — ل ره

This applies to the second and third movements only. If it applied to all of them, the movement through a vacuum would take no time, and the problem would remain. The argument first assumes that movement has a definite time of its own, since it assigns a duration to movement through a vacuum. It then denies that movement has a duration of its own, making its time depend on the resistance in the path. The contradiction comes from combining these two claims. — The Teacher.

Expansion means that a vacuum forms between the body's parts; contraction means that the vacuum disappears. The reply denies that these are the only possible explanations: a body may expand by growing larger after being smaller, or contract by shrinking. — Ismail.
The second claim can also be disproved by this argument, as the author's closing line indicates: a directional push would conflict with the claim that all parts of a vacuum are alike. — Ismail.

This is true when the cause of a whole is directly and fully the cause of it as a whole. Otherwise, a cause need not cause every part of what it produces. A carpenter, for example, makes a chair but does not separately make all its parts. — Ismail.

In the usual technical sense, “acting” means affecting something through a gradual process, and “being acted on” means undergoing such a process. The verb forms suggest an action continually renewed. This is why the author says in The Testimonies that neither of these categories contains motion. Each is a feature beyond the thing that acts or is acted on, so calling quality a “stable state” excludes them. As for the author’s second objection, there is no problem if a later condition in a definition also excludes what an earlier condition excluded, as the philosophers themselves acknowledge. — Isma‘il.

The definition could simply have said “a state which, when understood, does not require us to understand something else.” The familiar version adds the word “stable.” The author’s point is not that an earlier condition in a definition must do work that no later condition can do. Rather, this later condition already rules out the things that “stable” was supposed to exclude, so the added word does no further work. His next question, “What if it was added to exclude time?”, confirms this reading. — The teacher of Rasht.

The intended point is that qualities of the soul do not relate to bodies as quantities. If they relate to bodies at all, they do so because bodies have souls, not because of their quantity. — Isma‘il.

We can understand the phrase “qualities specific to quantity” to mean qualities that relate to bodies in a way that lets us consider them apart from souls. This kind of relation does not prevent such qualities from existing outside bodies too. — Isma‘il.
The kind that is not a readiness for completion, but is itself a completion, consists of qualities of the soul, which divide into temporary states and established traits. — Isma‘il.
Imam al-Razi says that if air were always perceptible, people would not doubt that it exists or imagine that the space between heaven and earth is completely empty. — Jalwa.
The claim in the first chapter was that color does not exist; this claim is that light does not exist. Keep the distinction in mind. — Jalwa.
He means that a lack of light makes the reflected brightness weak, which keeps the color from appearing. Think about it. — Ismail.
These words seem to make darkness and light opposites by simple denial and affirmation, rather than by absence and possession, as some other accounts say. Think carefully. — Ismail.

The wave is called the nearest cause of sound because it always accompanies sound: where one exists, so does the other, and where one is absent, so is the other. Al-Razi says this connection gives us only a likely explanation, while the question needs certainty. The reply is that examining many individual cases, together with strong insight, can show with certainty that sound is caused by a particular kind of wave in the air. — Ismail.

I say that this explanation seems to imply that hearing a sound does not require the air carrying it to reach the eardrum. If a particular wave has already produced sound in the air, and the soul is connected—even indirectly—to the air touching the body, the soul should be able to hear that sound. We have assumed that this connection is enough for the soul to perceive, through the appropriate sense, whatever happens in the air and can be sensed by that faculty. Sound would seem to meet that condition. Unless, that is, we say the soul cannot hear sound until the air carrying it reaches the eardrum. Consider this carefully. — Isma‘il.

The difference between a “station on the path” and a “spiritual station” is like the difference between a state and a settled habit. The Persian verse says: “From the Beloved’s door to the Kaaba of the heart, lovers have a thousand and one stations.” — Ismail.

God is not a possible being. Just as He is necessary in Himself, so He is necessary in every respect, and everything proceeds from Him. The word “possible” can also be used in a broader sense: in God, it means necessity in Himself; in a contingent being, it means possibility in itself. Consider this carefully. — Ismail.

Will has one reality, but degrees and levels that differ. Each degree and level gives the word “will” a somewhat different meaning. In that sense, all the definitions given for will are right in their own way. This will be explained in the discussion of divine things. — Ismail.

Yet awareness of the pleasant thing is still present. If pleasure were simply awareness of what suits us, then pleasure should not cease when the condition has settled. But if pleasure consists in leaving an unnatural condition, that movement ends when the new condition becomes settled; on that account, the pleasure ends with it. — Isma‘il.

He treats awareness of what naturally suits a faculty as equivalent to its pleasure. On this basis he reverses the general statement “Every pleasure is awareness of the perfection proper to the faculty that perceives it,” and says, “Every awareness of what is natural to a faculty is pleasure for that faculty.” Do not overlook this step. — Isma‘il.

If the mental image is wholly different from separation, it cannot oppose continuity, which is a perfection, and cannot be pain. If it is identical with separation, then it is the object known outside the perceiver, not knowledge, and still cannot be pain. Consider this carefully. — Isma‘il.

At times, a disturbed bodily mixture directly causes pain, and the break in continuity that follows causes pain only indirectly. At other times, the relationship is reversed. A settled mixture causes no pain, directly or indirectly, because it is not felt. — Isma‘il.
A thing’s evil may be described as something it has, or as something it lacks if evil is itself an absence. So being evil in itself does not mean that it has no existence. — Isma‘il.

The author holds that the sensed form present to the soul is one with the perceiving substance. If that first sensed form ceases, how can it still be present to the soul? One possible answer is that it has ceased in time but remains present in the timeless order. Consider this carefully. — Isma‘il

I say: a careful thinker will see that greater resistance means less change in the sense organ, and therefore weaker perception and sensation. Pleasure and pain should also be weaker, contrary to the physician’s account. — Isma‘il

When this spirit forms in the liver, it is called the natural spirit; when it forms in the heart, the vital spirit; and when it forms in the brain, the spirit of the soul. The natural spirit carries the body’s natural powers, the vital spirit its animal powers, and the psychic spirit its powers of the soul. — Isma‘il

Existence is one reality with levels that differ in perfection. What is more complete reflects what is less complete in a fuller way, while what is less complete reflects what is more complete in a more limited way. This is why people say that a cause tells us fully what its effect is, while an effect tells us only part of what its cause is. Think about this. — Isma‘il

If the confusion is explained this way—that shape is a form of a thing because it relates to something outside it, namely its boundary, while position is also a form of a thing because it relates to what is outside it—then shape would count as position. The first and second points below would not answer the confusion; only the third would. Consider this carefully. — Isma‘il
That is, a genuine relation, not merely a relation in the broader, commonly used sense. — Isma‘il

Two opposites must take turns in one and the same individual subject, and they cannot be present in it together. For a quality to be stronger or weaker, its subject must be able to pass from one degree to another and remain the same. The subject of this kind of quality cannot remain the same through such a change, so the quality has no greater or lesser degree. Reflect on this. — Isma‘il

Two opposites must be positive features that take turns in the same subject and cannot exist together in the same respect. Even and odd do not fit, because oddness is negative. And if oddness were positive, it still would not take turns with evenness in the same individual number. This gives another argument based on the first condition. Consider it carefully. — Isma‘il

Attributes have only two of the four causes of existence: an acting cause and a purpose. They do not have the causes that make up their essence: matter and form, or the general kind and the feature that distinguishes it. The difference between matter and a general kind, and between form and a defining feature, depends on how we consider them. What has no matter has no general kind; what has no form has no defining feature. Attributes have no matter or form in outside reality, so they are simple there, though the mind can analyze them into a general meaning and a specific one. Some say that the mind can do this without there being matter and form in the outside world. On that view, attributes can be composed in thought while remaining simple in reality. The majority's point is that attributes lack outside matter and form, since they clearly have general and specific features. In the standard account, there are nine highest categories of attributes. — Isma‘il
An essential feature is clear only when the thing is known fully and in detail. It is not certain that both conditions are met in the case being discussed. Think it over. — Isma‘il

The defense says that the definition describes something like a specific kind by means of something like a general kind, and that “relative” is used in both ordinary and technical speech for the defined idea and for its definition. The objection is that although a compound relative includes the simple relation, it is not broader in the way a general kind is broader than a specific one. It includes the simple relation as a whole includes a part. So the circularity remains. Consider this carefully. — Isma‘il
This works if what defines the concept applies to it only incidentally, or if what is being defined—the particular example—is itself known in some respect. Think it over. — Isma‘il

Earlier there was a denial that the later time exists. When the later time comes into being, that earlier denial no longer holds. The mind thus understands a former absence as something that is no longer present. Consider this carefully. — Isma‘il
He specifies a simple thing because, in a compound, the general kind and the defining feature have distinct existences outside the mind, as matter and form. Consider this carefully. — Isma‘il

Someone might say that a statement about the outside world requires the subject and its feature to be joined outside the mind, but not that the feature itself exist there. For example, “Zayd is blind.” I answer that the feature must exist there in some way, though its existence may be weak and dependent, not independent. This was explained earlier in the discussion of general matters. — Isma‘il

God's presence with things is His sustaining presence, not a presence in time. It is eternal and continuous. The things He sustains are not lacking or passing away in relation to Him, even if they are so in themselves. Understand this carefully. — Isma‘il

Zayd's being Amr's neighbor is not like Amr's being Zayd's father. The two people are enough to identify the fatherhood, but they do not identify their particular neighborly relation: their houses may be next door, or they may be separated by forty houses. To identify that relation, we must specify both houses. — Isma‘il

“First,” “second,” and “third” refer to the three meanings just listed: the feature itself, the thing it describes, and the two together. “Category” means one of the ten basic kinds of things, since the thing being described belongs to one of them. Consider this carefully. — Isma‘il

The relation to a place is not an added feature of the nature of “where”; it belongs to a body because of its “where.” So a body's relation to a place is something added to its existence in itself. This differs from blackness's relation to a body, which is simply how blackness exists. But the relation of “where” to a body is like that of blackness to a body. Understand this. — Isma‘il

The relation itself to time, to one of its limits, or to something connected with time is not “when.” Rather, “when” is a state that gives rise to this relation for a thing that exists in time. — Isma‘il
Considering connection excludes number; considering something fixed and stable excludes time. The quantities that have position are line, surface, and geometrical body. — Isma‘il

That is, at the level of the concept. In reality, God's outpouring of existence is necessary. It is called His mercy to all worlds, His will, His all-embracing mercy, the Real by which things are created, the Breath of the All-Merciful, and other names. — Isma‘il

The agent acts on the recipient through its act, but it acts on its act through its own essence, not through another act. The hadith says: “Things were created through will, and will was created through itself.” Understand the point. — Isma‘il

In that case, the substance is composed of matter, which is the soul, and an intellectual form. It is not a body; its part is neither a material form nor matter. This shows the flaw in the first division. On the second division there is no flaw: while the substance is connected to the body it is a soul, and afterward it is an intellect. Consider this carefully. — Isma‘il

If “soul” means animal soul, there is no difference between the second and third cases; if it means rational soul, there is no difference between the second and fourth. One might argue that animal soul is intended, and that the second case considers the existence of an animal and the soul as part of its existence, while the third considers the meaning of body and the soul as part of its meaning. Perhaps the author says “part of what makes it what it is” in the second case and “part of its essence's meaning” in the third to point to this difference. Understand the point. — Isma‘il

By “thing” in the phrase “exists in a thing,” the author means something that exists outside the mind. So the definition of accident does not apply to a body being in some place or time in general, or to a human being being in some general end or purpose. These two kinds of presence are excluded by the words “in a thing.” Consider this. — Isma‘il

This is questionable in light of what the author says at the end of the Metaphysics. In his account of the world's origination, he establishes that change and renewal in bodies, and their belonging to the category of “when,” are formal and substantial features that constitute them, or constitute what their existence and individuality require, or belong to the level of their existence and individuality. They are not accidents from which a body could in reality be separated or free. A body's relation to being in time would then be like matter's relation to form. Do not overlook this. — Isma‘il
So denying motion at an instant is not rest, since rest cannot be predicated of motion: opposites cannot apply to one another. Consider this. — Isma‘il
The celestial body's inability to leave its place is because leaving it would require straight-line motion, which is impossible for celestial natures, as established in its proper place. — Isma‘il

You know that a feature is something that follows its subject in a way that describes it and is affected by it. This applies to form in relation to matter, not to matter in relation to form. — Isma‘il

On this account, it is difficult to say that form inheres in matter, since an inhering thing's existence in itself is identical with its existence for its subject, not with the existence of its subject. Consider this. — Isma‘il

The point of this argument is that universal substances are the essence of a particular substance, and the essence of a particular substance is a substance; therefore universal substances are substances. The major premise is explained by analyzing the particular substance into its individual identity and essence. If its substantiality comes from its individual identity, then no other individual would be a substance, which is impossible. So it must come from its essence. The answer is that, if “essence” in the claim “universal substances are the essence of a particular substance” means the unrestricted essence, or natural universal, the minor premise is false: universal substances are concepts understood from individuals, and no understood essence is the unrestricted essence of individuals. If “essence” means the essence as understood, the minor premise is true, but the major premise is false: the essence as understood is not an analytic part of individuals, so their substantiality does not come from it. It comes from the unrestricted essence, which is an analytic part of individuals. If the meaning changes between the two premises, the middle term has not been repeated, and the conclusion does not follow. Consider this. — Isma‘il
By primary predication. So when one understands a kind of substance, such as human, what is known is substance—that is, substance is included in its definition. — Jalwah.

Essence considered in itself is neither substance nor accident; it is not an instance of either. If it exists in a way that is not in a subject, it is substance; if it exists in a subject, it is accident. I would add that philosophers say all categories are of the order of essences, and that substance and accident are of that order; the author says so too. How, then, can there be an essence that is neither substance nor accident? Also, the essence of substance in the outside world is substance, since the definition of substance truly applies to it. If it enters the mind in its true reality and is then said to be neither substance nor accident in itself, it would have changed from substance into neither substance nor accident. Jalwah.

Avicenna says in the Metaphysics of The Healing: “The essence of substance is substance in the sense that it exists in reality without being in a subject; this essence is understood from something whose existence in reality is not in a subject. Its existence in the intellect in this way, however, is not part of the definition of substance: the definition does not say that it exists in the intellect without being in a subject. Rather, its definition says that whether or not it exists in the intellect, its existence in reality is not in a subject.” If someone says, “The intellect is also part of reality,” the answer is that “reality” here means a place in which substance, when present, produces its actions and effects. If someone says, “Then you have made the essence of substance sometimes an accident and sometimes a substance, after denying that this is possible,” we reply that we have also denied that the same essence can exist in reality sometimes as an accident needing a subject and sometimes as a substance not needing one. We have not denied that its intelligible concept becomes an accident—that is, exists in the soul, not as a part. The change is not in the essence itself, which would imply that it had changed into its opposite. The change is in the existence, which is distinct from essence. Jalwah.

A thing is either existent by its essence, in which case it is necessary; nonexistent by its essence, in which case it is impossible; or neither existent nor nonexistent by its essence, in which case it is possible. Since Zayd is possible, he is neither existent nor nonexistent considered only as human essence. This does not make him nonexistent in that respect, because a possible thing can lack both opposites at a given level, as explained in the discussion of essence. Consider this. — Isma‘il

The soul has two aspects: its existence in itself and its existence for another. In the first respect, it falls under substance as a species under its broader kind. In the second, substance is a general feature of it, because in that respect the soul is a form, identical in reality with its difference though distinct in how we consider it. A broader kind is a general feature in relation to a difference; since a form is identical in reality with its difference, broader kind is also a general feature in relation to it. We make this point specifically about the soul because, unlike other forms imprinted in matter, its existence in itself differs from its existence for another: because it is immaterial, it does not cease to exist when the body perishes. Notice this. — Isma‘il, teacher of our divine teacher.

The shared meaning of substance, predicated of substances in one sense, is explained by Imam Fakhr al-Din as the third meaning: an essence that, once it exists, has the property of independence from a subject. He then makes this meaning particular to each substance and uses that to deny that the third meaning is shared, whether essentially or accidentally. Is this not a clear contradiction? Unless he means that the concept is shared as a description, while the thing described is particular in each case. But then he would still have to explain how one meaning can be drawn from things that differ precisely as different things—a point already shown to be impossible. Consider this. — Isma‘il
That is, the broader kind does not apply to the simple part because the part is identical with the meaning of the broader kind. Do not overlook this. — Isma‘il

The right answer to the second objection is to choose its second option: by “species” and “broader kind,” we mean the natural species and natural broader kind. These exist outside the mind through the very existence of their individuals. An individual is more fully present in time than a natural species or broader kind, since it exists in itself while the species and broader kind exist by being predicated of it and united with it. Likewise, a species is more fully realized in the eternal order than a broader kind: the broader kind is wholly indeterminate, while the species is determinate in that order, though indeterminate in time; the individual is not indeterminate. This is what it means to say that individual, species, and broader kind differ in their existence. The author’s reply would apply only if the objection concerned degrees of substantiality. But the objection is explicitly about degrees of existence and of being existent. Consider this carefully. — Isma‘il

Universal substances are determinate in the mind but indeterminate in the outside world. Each universal has its own distinct existence in the mind, though it applies to all its external individuals. So it can be pointed to intellectually in view of its mental existence and determination, but not in view of its external indeterminacy. The objector has confused external indeterminacy with mental determination. Consider this. — Isma‘il

The fourth argument differs from the third only in being broader and more specific about why a part of a substantial compound is a substance. The third says that it is part of a substance, and a part of a substance is a substance. The fourth says that a part of a substance is not an accident in it, and whatever is not an accident is a substance. Consider this. — Isma‘il

A natural compound must have a need between its parts, without a circular dependence. A natural compound cannot be made from an accident and its subject: although the accident needs the subject, the subject does not need the accident. Their combination is therefore only conceptual, not natural. This shows that the confusion came from mixing up a conceptual whole with a natural compound. Do not overlook this. — Isma‘il
